paper_metadata.title: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo: an imaginary-time method for real-time quantum dynamics

summary: The paper introduces Clock Quantum Monte Carlo, a classical simulation method combining the Feynman–Kitaev clock Hamiltonian with FCIQMC to simulate quantum circuit dynamics. Demonstrations include synthetic circuits with 11 qubits and 128 time steps and show parallel efficiencies of about 95% with 2 processors and about 70% with 8 processors on a CPU cluster. The work focuses on mitigating the dynamical sign problem using time-dependent basis rotations.

experiments.description: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo applied to gate-based quantum circuit dynamics using the Feynman-Kitaev clock construction, with numerical examples on local rotations and circuits containing CNOT gates; includes time-dependent basis rotations to mitigate the sign problem and a parallel-in-time implementation.

algorithm.variant: FCIQMC applied to the Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian for quantum dynamics
algorithm.convergence_criteria: simulation time evolved until walker population equilibrates; observables averaged after equilibration
algorithm.parameter_initialization: walkers initialized from the chosen initial state |0⟩⊗N and circuit-defined history state; basis-rotation scheme initialized from local circuit rotations when used

problem_formulation.encoding_details: system basis states |i⟩ combined with discrete time register |t⟩ in the Clock Hamiltonian; circuit dynamics encoded as history state over time steps
problem_formulation.objective_function: minimize the Clock Hamiltonian ground state energy corresponding to the history state of the unitary evolution
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: penalty operator C0 fixes the initial state at t=0

problem_instance.description: Quantum circuit dynamics examples: single-qubit local rotations and circuits with varying numbers of CNOT gates; one benchmark uses 11 qubits and 128 time points

dataset_specification.description: synthetic quantum circuits; local rotation R(θ) and circuits with controlled-NOT gates

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: expectation value ⟨S_z⟩ at final time versus mean number of walkers; multiple rotation angles and gate counts compared; strong-scaling benchmark on 11-qubit, 128-time-point instance

hardware.device_name: Linux cluster with AMD Opteron 6376 CPUs

noise_model.error_mitigation_method: time-dependent basis rotations to mitigate the sign problem

implementation_details.classical_solver: FCIQMC / interacting-walker Monte Carlo on classical computer
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: basis rotations Bt chosen from circuit structure; for local rotations Bt = Q_{t'<t} U_{t'} with multi-qubit gates replaced by identity in the approximate scheme
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: time-averaged observables with autocorrelation correction; annihilation of walkers; parallel domain decomposition in time

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: sharp transition from sign-incoherent to sign-coherent sampling as walker number increases

speedup_claims.factor: over 95% parallel efficiency with 2 processors; 70% with 8 processors
speedup_claims.conditions: strong scaling on an 11-qubit, 128-time-point simulation using a simple MPI implementation on a commodity cluster
speedup_claims.caveats: Efficiency is reported for a specific benchmark and implementation; not a general algorithmic speedup.

speedup_claims.conditions: from the strong-scaling plot on a commodity Linux cluster for the reported benchmark
speedup_claims.caveats: Exact value is estimated from the figure; the paper text does not state the maximum speedup numerically.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: not explicitly given; sign problem can make required walkers scale exponentially in general

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not applicable; the work proposes a classical Monte Carlo algorithm (FCIQMC) for simulating quantum circuit dynamics using the Feynman–Kitaev clock Hamiltonian.
